Jeremy Tuloup

JupyterLite: a Jupyter distribution that runs entirely in the web browser, without any server components

Kernels in WebAssembly

Python, R, C++ and more, running on the user's device (Pyodide, xeus).

Just static files

HTML, JavaScript and Wasm. Any web server or CDN, no backend to run.

Built from JupyterLab

The JupyterLab and Notebook interfaces you know, with their extensions.

JupyterLab: an application made of plugins

A core application object and a set of extensions.
  • Extensions provide nearly every feature, from notebooks to the file browser
  • A core design decision from the very beginning
  • Pick a different set of plugins, get a different application

What if the server parts ran in the browser too?

p5-notebook March 2020

  • A minimal notebook UI for p5.js kernels
  • Built from JupyterLab componentsJupyterLab 2.0, released three weeks earlier
  • A tiny Jupyter "server" running in the browsercontents, kernels, kernelspecs, sessions
  • "This is still an experiment"

Prior art

Iodide notebook 2017

A notebook made for the browser at Mozilla, with its own interface and file format

Pyodide was created for it in 2018

github.com/iodide-project/iodide

Jyve 2018

Kernels running in the browser, as a JupyterLab extension, by Nicholas Bollweg

JavaScript, TypeScript, CoffeeScript, Brython, p5.js

github.com/deathbeds/jyve

Keep the components, swap the backend

It relies on a very minimal Jupyter Server that also runs in the browser [...] This makes it easier to reuse components from core JupyterLab and swap the backend to an alternative one running in the browser.

Kernels: p5.js code evaluated in an iframe. No Python anywhere.

Combining two ideas

JupyterLab Classic

An alternative JupyterLab distribution, reusing the JupyterLab plugins in another application

+

p5-notebook

The server in the browser: contents, kernels and sessions, in the tab

JupyterLite

A JupyterLab distribution that runs entirely in the browser, with the JupyterLab and Classic interfaces, from April 2021

First commit 27 March 2021

JupyterLite is a JupyterLab distribution that runs entirely in the browser without a Jupyter Server.

One year after p5-notebook, almost to the day, and four months after JupyterLab Classic.

Python via Pyodide, in a Web Worker April 2021

Boots in seconds

  • First release on PyPI0.1.0a0 · 2 June 2021
  • A static site, a Python kernel, no install

Going public 13 July 2021

  • Announced on the Jupyter blog: "JupyterLite: Jupyter ❤️ WebAssembly ❤️ Python"
  • Widgets, Altair, Plotly, real-time collaboration
  • README status: "the project is still unofficial"

JupyterLite in the wild

Websites, documentation, classrooms, locked-down machines, and platforms built on top.

jupyter.org/try: from Binder to static files

2021 · mybinder.org

A server per click

  • The try links drive a large share of mybinder.org traffic
  • ~25,000 sessions a day from the first two links
  • Up to 90% of launches rejected at peak times
→
March 2022 · JupyterLite

Nothing to launch

  • JupyterLab and Notebook served as static files
  • Starts in seconds, for everyone
  • No per-user server to schedule or pay for
~400k

unique visitors per month on the JupyterLite deployments of jupyter.org/try

Using the same approach as JupyterLite: running Python in the browser with Pyodide

Offline and locked-down environments

  • Only a browser: no install, no admin rights
  • Serve from an intranet, a laptop, a USB stick
  • Exams in a secured browser (Moodle + Safe Exam Browser)
  • Code and data stay on the device
# a fully self-contained site
$ pip install jupyterlite-core
$ jupyter lite build
$ jupyter lite archive
# → one tarball, no external requests

notebook.link January 2026

  • Built on JupyterLite: share a notebook with a link
  • Python, R, C++, Octavexeus kernels, packages from Emscripten Forge
  • Terminal and AI assistant included

03

Scale, cost and limits

Only static files

Server-based

● a user  ·  ▭ a server running their kernels

Cost grows with users. One kernel per user on a server, capacity planning, autoscaling.

JupyterLite

○ a user whose device runs the code

static files · CDN

Cost grows with bandwidth. Code runs on each user's device, files are cached. GitHub Pages, ReadTheDocs, S3…

Thousands of concurrent users from a static website, with zero per-user server costs

Limitations

Packages
Must be compiled to WebAssembly (Pyodide, Emscripten Forge)
Resources
Memory and CPU bound by the browser and the device
Network
No raw sockets, requests subject to CORS
Storage
Files live in the browser, per device
First load
Tens of MB to download, then cached
Extensions
Bundled at build time, no server extensions

Complementary JupyterHub and Binder remain the right tools for heavy workloads, data on servers, GPUs.

04

What's next

Bridging the gap with JupyterLab

  • JupyterLite is becoming a set of JupyterLab extensions
  • 0.6: in-browser services as JupyterLab pluginsthe Service Manager became a plugin in JupyterLab 4.4
  • 0.9: the Extension Managerbuilt on a new JupyterLab 4.7 extension point
  • Upstream first: fixes land in JupyterLab, JupyterLite drops its workaroundse.g. drive-aware kernel sessions in JupyterLab 4.7
  • Hybrid kernels: server and browser side by side

More languages

Python, R, C++, GNU Octave, JavaScript, Lua

  • pip install and conda install at runtime
  • Numba in the browserLLVM IR compiled to WebAssembly at runtime

A shell in the browser

  • Commands compiled to WebAssembly
  • grep sed less vim nano git…
  • Packages from Emscripten Forge
  • Same file system as the notebooks

AI in Jupyter

  • Building blocks, the Jupyter wayeach piece is its own extension: install it, swap it, or write your own
  • Many setups from the same blocksa team server with frontier agents, a classroom with one assistant, JupyterLite with everything in the browser
  • Agents that work with notebooksedit and run cells, files and terminals, asking permission first
ChatShared with other people, saved as files
PersonasJupyternaut, or your own
AgentsClaude, Codex, Copilot, Gemini… through the Agent Client Protocol
ModelsHundreds of providers, or models running in the browser
ToolsNotebooks, files and terminals
MCP serversBring your own tools and data

Assistants in the browser

  • jupyterlite-ai: chat, completions, agent mode
  • Anthropic, OpenAI, Mistral, Google, any OpenAI-compatible API
  • MCP servers and skills
  • In-browser models: WebLLM, Transformers.js, Chrome built-in AI

A coding agent in the terminal

  • A jupyternaut command, like running a coding agent in a regular terminalopen pull request: jupyterlite/ai#373
  • Asks before running commands or changing files
  • Only the LLM calls leave the browser
js-shell: jupyternaut # alias: ai
# tools available to the agent
shell run a command in cockle
list_files list a directory
read_file read with line numbers
write_file create or overwrite
edit_file replace an exact string
